title: Syncope
subject: Medicine
summary: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion. Identify precipitating factors, assess severity, and rule out life‑threatening causes quickly, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery, caused by a temporary drop in cerebral blood flow.
b: Diagnose by history of rapid onset, short duration (<1 min), and full recovery.
Exclude seizures (post‑ictal confusion) and metabolic encephalopathy.

sections.p: Use the ESC/ACC risk stratification: high‑risk (cardiac cause, structural heart disease, exertional syncope), intermediate, and low‑risk (vasovagal, orthostatic).
b: High‑risk features: chest pain, exertional syncope, heart disease, abnormal ECG, trauma.
Low‑risk: clear trigger, prodrome, normal exam, no cardiac history.

sections.p: Classify by mechanism: cardiac, reflex (neurally mediated), orthostatic, and miscellaneous.
b: Cardiac: aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, acute MI, tamponade.
Reflex: vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, situational (cough, micturition).
Orthostatic: dehydration, autonomic failure, medication (diuretics, antihypertensives).
Miscellaneous: anemia, severe infection (malaria, TB sepsis), pulmonary embolism, sickle‑cell crisis.

sections.p: Patients report a prodrome (light‑headedness, nausea, sweating) followed by a brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery.
b: Prodrome present in reflex syncope; absent in cardiac arrhythmia.
Exertional syncope suggests fixed outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis) or severe pulmonary hypertension.

t.b: Detect arrhythmia, ischemia, conduction block; abnormal findings raise cardiac risk.
Answers if drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic on standing; positive suggests orthostatic cause.
Assesses valve disease, LV function, pericardial effusion; absence of equipment → refer or use bedside cardiac exam.
Identify anemia, electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycaemia; treat if abnormal.
Looks for pulmonary infiltrates, cardiomegaly, signs of PE; if unavailable, focus on clinical PE clues.

sections.p: Immediate danger arises from cardiac causes, massive PE, aortic stenosis, or severe dehydration.
b: Syncope with chest pain, dyspnoea, or palpitations.
Traumatic injury from fall.
Persistent hypotension after the event.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, ensure safety, and monitor for recurrence.
b: Cardiac: urgent cardiology referral, consider anti‑arrhythmic or valve replacement; avoid β‑blockers in severe aortic stenosis without specialist input.
Reflex: education, physical counter‑pressure maneuvers, avoid triggers; midodrine if severe orthostatic intolerance.
Orthostatic: fluid repletion, review diuretics/antihypertensives, compression stockings.
Infection‑related: treat malaria, TB, or sepsis promptly; correct anemia.

sections.p: Arrange review within 1 week for high‑risk patients; low‑risk can be outpatient after discharge.
b: Educate on trigger avoidance, hydration, and when to call emergency services.
Repeat ECG and orthostatic vitals at follow‑up.

sections.p: Distinguish syncope from seizures, transient ischemic attack, and metabolic encephalopathy.
b: Seizure: post‑ictal confusion, tongue biting, urinary incontinence.
TIA: focal neurological deficit lasting >5 min, no rapid recovery.
Hypoglycaemia: low glucose with neuroglycopenic symptoms, treat with glucose.

sections.p: Normal ECG does not exclude cardiac syncope; orthostatic vitals can be falsely normal if patient is supine too long.
b: Intermittent arrhythmias may need Holter or event monitor.
Mild anemia may still cause syncope in severe malaria.

whenToSeekHelp: Syncope with chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnoea
Persistent low blood pressure or altered mental state after the event

faq.q: Why does exertional syncope suggest aortic stenosis?
faq.a: Exercise raises demand; a fixed valve cannot increase output, causing cerebral hypoperfusion.

faq.q: Can a normal ECG rule out a cardiac cause?
faq.a: No; intermittent arrhythmias or structural disease may be missed without further testing.

faq.q: What bedside maneuver helps a vasovagal episode?
faq.a: Leg crossing and muscle tensing increase venous return and prevent fainting.

exam: What immediate investigations are mandatory in a patient with syncope on exertion? — ECG, orthostatic BP, focused cardiac exam, and bedside ultrasound if possible; they identify cardiac obstruction or arrhythmia.
How would you differentiate vasovagal syncope from a cardiac arrhythmia at the bedside? — Look for prodrome, trigger, and examine pulse; absence of prodrome and irregular pulse point to arrhythmia.
A 55‑year‑old with known aortic stenosis faints while climbing stairs. What is the next step? — Treat as high‑risk cardiac syncope; arrange urgent cardiology review for possible valve replacement.

Why is midodrine preferred over fludrocortisone for chronic orthostatic syncope in low‑resource settings? — Midodrine works quickly without causing fluid overload, which is safer where monitoring is limited.
What red‑flag symptom would make you suspect pulmonary embolism in a syncope patient? — Sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hypotension.

Explain why a patient on antihypertensives may develop orthostatic syncope after a diarrhoeal illness. — Volume loss plus medication‑induced vasodilation reduces standing BP, leading to cerebral hypoperfusion.
How does sickle‑cell crisis precipitate syncope? — Severe anaemia and vaso‑occlusion reduce oxygen delivery, causing cerebral hypoperfusion.
What is the role of compression stockings in syncope management? — They improve venous return, reducing orthostatic drops in blood pressure.
